body:
How does a nuclear power plant produce energy?

A nuclear power plant generates electricity by using heat released during controlled nuclear reactions. Unlike a coal-based thermal power station, it does not burn coal to produce this heat. Instead, it uses the energy stored within atomic nuclei.

The basic principle is straightforward: nuclear fission releases heat, the heat is used to produce steam, and the steam rotates a turbine connected to an electrical generator.

The distinctive feature of a nuclear power plant is therefore its source of heat. The conversion of that heat into electricity follows the same broad principle used in many conventional thermal power stations.

Central principle: A nuclear reactor produces heat through controlled nuclear fission. The turbine and generator convert that heat into electricity through an intermediate mechanical process.

Understanding the atomic nucleus

Every atom contains a small central nucleus consisting of protons and, except in hydrogen-1 (protium), neutrons. Electrons occupy the region surrounding the nucleus.

  • Protons: Positively charged particles inside the nucleus.
  • Neutrons: Electrically neutral particles inside the nucleus.
  • Electrons: Negatively charged particles surrounding the nucleus.

The number of protons determines the element. Uranium has an atomic number of 92, meaning that every uranium nucleus contains 92 protons.

Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. Such atoms are called isotopes.

Uranium-235 and uranium-238

Two important isotopes of uranium are uranium-235 (U-235) and uranium-238 (U-238).

Both contain 92 protons, but U-235 contains 143 neutrons, whereas U-238 contains 146 neutrons. Their mass numbers are therefore different.

The distinction matters because U-235 readily undergoes fission after absorbing a slow neutron. U-238 does not readily undergo fission with slow neutrons.

Natural uranium contains approximately 0.7% U-235, with most of the remainder being U-238. Some reactor types can use natural uranium, while others require uranium in which the proportion of U-235 has been increased.

What is radioactivity?

Radioactivity is the spontaneous transformation of an unstable atomic nucleus, generally accompanied by the emission of radiation. The nucleus changes without requiring an external neutron to initiate that particular decay.

Three familiar types of radiation associated with radioactive decay are:

  • Alpha radiation: Consists of particles containing 2 protons and 2 neutrons, equivalent to helium nuclei.
  • Beta radiation: Consists of energetic particles, commonly electrons, emitted during certain nuclear transformations.
  • Gamma radiation: Consists of high-energy electromagnetic radiation.

Radioactivity and nuclear fission are related but are not identical. Radioactive decay is a spontaneous nuclear transformation, whereas the fission reactions used to sustain power production in most nuclear reactors are induced by neutron absorption.

Many products of nuclear fission are radioactive. Their subsequent decay is important for reactor safety because they continue releasing radiation and heat even after the main fission chain reaction has been stopped.

Do not confuse the processes: Ordinary radioactive decay does not require an incoming neutron. The principal heat source during normal nuclear power generation is the controlled fission of fuel nuclei.

Prelims focus

  • Uranium has atomic number 92.
  • U-235 contains 92 protons and 143 neutrons.
  • U-238 contains 92 protons and 146 neutrons.
  • Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
  • Natural uranium contains approximately 0.7% U-235.
  • Trap: Radioactivity and neutron-induced nuclear fission are not synonymous.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, chapter 4, 'Structure of the Atom', sections 4.5–4.6, printed pp. 52–53; NCERT, Science, Class 10, 2020–21 edition, chapter 14, 'Sources of Energy', section 14.3.4, printed pp. 251–252; International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), 'Fundamentals of Nuclear Power', sections 'Types of Radiation' and 'Nuclear Fission', consulted 16 November 2026; IAEA, Nuclear Fuel Cycle Information System, sections 'Enrichment' and 'Electricity', consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Nuclear Energy: The Science Behind a Nuclear Power Plant

body:
What happens during nuclear fission?

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into lighter nuclei, accompanied by the release of energy.

In a typical fission event involving U-235, the nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes unstable. It then splits into 2 lighter nuclei, called fission fragments. The process releases a large amount of energy and usually 2 or 3 neutrons.

The precise fission fragments can vary from one event to another. However, the important result remains the same: a heavy nucleus divides, energy is released, and additional neutrons become available.

The fission fragments move with considerable energy. As they interact with surrounding material, their kinetic energy is transferred to the fuel and becomes heat.

Why does fission release so much energy?

The combined mass of the fission products and other released particles is slightly less than the total mass before the reaction. This difference corresponds to the energy released.

Albert Einstein's mass-energy relationship expresses the principle:

\(E = \Delta m c^{2}\)

Here, E represents the released energy, the magnitude of Δm represents the mass difference, and c is the speed of light in a vacuum.

Because the speed of light is extremely large, a small mass difference can correspond to a substantial amount of energy.

This explains the high energy density of nuclear fuel compared with ordinary chemical fuels. In chemical combustion, the reactions mainly involve the rearrangement of electrons and chemical bonds. Nuclear fission involves changes within the atomic nucleus.

How does a chain reaction develop?

Some neutrons released during one fission event can enter other fissile nuclei and produce further fissions. Those subsequent fissions release additional neutrons, allowing the process to repeat.

This continuing sequence is called a nuclear chain reaction.

  1. A neutron is absorbed by a U-235 nucleus.
  2. The nucleus undergoes fission and releases energy.
  3. Additional neutrons emerge from the fission event.
  4. Some of these neutrons cause further fissions.
  5. The repeated process produces a continuing supply of heat.

What makes a chain reaction controlled?

A useful power reactor must maintain a chain reaction at a regulated rate. It must not simply allow the number of fissions to increase without control.

The term critical has a specific meaning in reactor science: the chain reaction is self-sustaining. When a reactor operates steadily at a constant power level, neutron production and losses are balanced so that the overall fission rate remains approximately constant.

Three related terms help clarify this condition:

  • Subcritical: The neutron population and associated fission chain tend to decrease without an additional source.
  • Critical: The chain reaction is self-sustaining, allowing a steady operating condition.
  • Supercritical: The neutron population and fission rate tend to increase. In a power reactor, changes in reactivity are regulated to control the resulting power change.

These terms describe the behaviour of a nuclear chain reaction. Critical does not mean that a nuclear explosion is occurring.

Why are slow neutrons important?

Neutrons released by fission are initially energetic. In a thermal-neutron reactor, slowing these neutrons increases their likelihood of causing further fission in U-235.

A special material called a moderator performs this slowing function. It helps sustain the required chain reaction without itself serving as the nuclear fuel.

Not every reactor uses a moderator. The explanation here concerns the thermal-neutron reactors commonly used for electricity generation, including India's pressurised heavy-water reactors.

Fission releases neutrons; the neutrons can continue the chain reaction; the moderator helps slow them; and the reactor's control arrangements regulate the reaction rate.

Prelims focus

  • Neutron-induced fission of U-235 produces lighter nuclei, energy and additional neutrons.
  • A chain reaction continues when released neutrons initiate further fissions.
  • The moderator slows neutrons in a thermal-neutron reactor.
  • A critical reactor sustains a chain reaction.
  • The relationship \(E = \Delta m c^{2}\) expresses the conversion of a mass difference into energy.
  • Trap: A critical reactor is not necessarily undergoing an uncontrolled increase in power.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, 2020–21 edition, chapter 14, 'Sources of Energy', section 14.3.4, printed p. 251; IAEA, 'Fundamentals of Nuclear Power', section 'Nuclear Fission', consulted 16 November 2026; IAEA, 'Glossary of terms', entries 'Chain Reaction', 'Critical' and 'Moderator', consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Neutrons released by one fission event can initiate further fissions.

title: Nuclear Fission and the Controlled Chain Reaction

body:
The reactor core is the source of heat

The nuclear reactor is the part of the power plant in which a controlled fission chain reaction produces heat.

The central region where the nuclear fuel is located is called the reactor core. Uranium fuel is commonly manufactured into solid fuel pellets enclosed within metal tubes or fuel elements. These are arranged so that heat can be removed during reactor operation.

Several components work together in a reactor, but they do not perform the same task. Understanding the difference between the moderator, coolant and control rods is essential.

Functions of the main reactor components

ComponentMain functionExamples
Nuclear fuelContains nuclei that undergo fission and release heatUranium containing U-235
ModeratorSlows fast neutrons to improve the continuation of fission in thermal reactorsOrdinary water, heavy water, graphite
CoolantRemoves heat from the reactor core and transfers it elsewhereOrdinary water, heavy water, suitable gases
Control rodsAbsorb neutrons to regulate the fission reactionMaterials containing boron or cadmium

Moderator: slowing down neutrons

When fission releases fast neutrons, a moderator slows them through interactions with its atoms. In many thermal reactors, slower neutrons have a greater probability of causing U-235 nuclei to undergo fission.

Heavy water is water containing deuterium, a heavier isotope of hydrogen. Its chemical formula is D2O. Ordinary water, also called light water, has the familiar formula H2O.

Both light water and heavy water can be used as neutron moderators in appropriate reactor types. Graphite is another moderator material.

A moderator is not a control rod. The main purpose of a moderator in a thermal reactor is to slow neutrons, whereas control rods absorb neutrons to regulate the reaction.

Coolant: carrying heat away

As fission continues, the fuel becomes hot. A coolant circulates through the reactor's heat-removal system and transfers this heat to the steam-producing part of the power plant.

The coolant's principal job is therefore heat transfer, not neutron absorption or electrical generation.

One substance may perform more than one function. In certain reactors, water acts as both a moderator and a coolant. This does not make the two functions identical.

Control rods: regulating the chain reaction

Control rods contain materials that readily absorb neutrons.

When neutron-absorbing control rods are inserted further into the core, fewer neutrons remain available to cause further fissions. This generally reduces the chain reaction rate. Withdrawing the rods has the opposite tendency, allowing more neutrons to participate in fission.

Control rods are therefore part of the means used to regulate reactor power. Other control and shutdown arrangements may also be used, depending on the reactor design.

India's pressurised heavy-water reactors

A major reactor type in India is the Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor (PHWR).

Indian PHWRs generally use natural uranium as fuel and heavy water as both moderator and coolant.

Heavy water is particularly useful because it can slow neutrons while absorbing relatively few of them. This helps a PHWR sustain a chain reaction using natural uranium, which contains only a small proportion of U-235.

Light-water reactors are also used internationally and in India. They generally use ordinary water as moderator and coolant but commonly require enriched uranium fuel.

Prelims focus

  • Fuel contains nuclei that release energy through fission.
  • A moderator slows neutrons in a thermal reactor.
  • A coolant removes heat from the reactor core.
  • Control rods absorb neutrons and regulate the reaction.
  • Indian PHWRs generally use natural uranium fuel and heavy water as moderator and coolant.
  • Trap: Heavy water is not the nuclear fuel in a PHWR.

[Sources: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), Corporate Profile 2025, section 'Long-Term Nuclear Power Programme of the Country', printed p. 3; US Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy, 'Nuclear 101: How Does a Nuclear Reactor Work?', published 19 May 2025, sections 'Nuclear Fission Creates Heat' and 'Types of Light-Water Reactors', consulted 16 November 2026; IAEA, 'Glossary of terms', entries 'Control Rod', 'Coolant' and 'CANDU Reactor', consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Inside a Nuclear Reactor: Fuel, Moderator, Coolant and Control Rods

body:
The reactor does not produce electricity directly

Although nuclear fission occurs inside the reactor, electricity is produced by a separate machine called a generator.

The reactor's immediate output is heat. That heat is transferred through a working fluid to produce steam, which drives a turbine. The turbine, in turn, rotates the generator.

The complete energy transformation is:

Nuclear energy → Thermal energy → Mechanical energy → Electrical energy.

The main steps in electricity generation

  1. Heat production: Controlled fission takes place in the reactor core and heats the nuclear fuel.
  2. Heat removal: The reactor coolant absorbs heat from the fuel and carries it away from the core.
  3. Steam production: Heat is used to convert water into steam. In some reactor types, this happens in a steam generator through heat transfer from a separate primary coolant circuit.
  4. Turbine rotation: Steam passes through a turbine, transferring energy to its blades and causing the turbine shaft to rotate.
  5. Electricity generation: The turbine drives a generator, which converts mechanical rotation into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.
  6. Condensation and reuse: After leaving the turbine, steam is cooled and condensed back into water. The water can then be returned to the steam-production system.

Why do some reactors have separate water circuits?

In a pressurised-water reactor, the water circulating through the reactor core is maintained under pressure so that it remains liquid while becoming hot. It transfers its heat to a separate water circuit in a steam generator.

The second circuit produces steam that drives the turbine. The primary coolant and the secondary water transfer heat without normally mixing.

This broad separation of reactor cooling and steam production is also characteristic of pressurised heavy-water reactor arrangements.

However, not all nuclear plants produce steam in this manner. In a boiling-water reactor, water boils inside the reactor itself, and the resulting steam is directed towards the turbine.

Important distinction: A separate steam generator is common in pressurised-water and pressurised heavy-water arrangements, but it is not a universal feature of every nuclear reactor.

What do the condenser and cooling system do?

After steam has passed through the turbine, the condenser removes heat and turns the steam back into water. This permits the water-steam cycle to continue.

The power station also needs a way to discharge unwanted heat to its surroundings. Depending on the site, the cooling arrangement may use cooling towers, a water body or other suitable systems.

Cooling towers do not contain the nuclear fission reaction. They are associated with the removal of waste heat. A nuclear power plant does not necessarily need the familiar large cooling towers often shown in photographs.

How is a nuclear station different from a coal-based station?

Both nuclear and coal-based steam power stations use heat to produce steam, rotate turbines and drive generators.

The principal difference is the heat source:

  • Coal-based thermal station: Heat is produced by the chemical combustion of coal.
  • Nuclear station: Heat is produced primarily by controlled nuclear fission.

Consequently, a nuclear station does not require the continuous burning of fossil fuel in its reactor to produce heat.

Prelims focus

  • The reactor produces heat, not electricity directly.
  • Steam rotates the turbine; the turbine drives the generator.
  • The generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  • Pressurised-water reactors generally use separate primary and steam-producing water circuits.
  • Boiling-water reactors produce steam directly within the reactor vessel.
  • Trap: A cooling tower is not the site of nuclear fission.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, 2020–21 edition, chapter 14, 'Sources of Energy', sections 14.2.2 and 14.3.4, printed pp. 244–245 and 251; US Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy, 'Nuclear 101: How Does a Nuclear Reactor Work?', published 19 May 2025, sections 'Pressurized Water Reactors' and 'Boiling Water Reactors', consulted 16 November 2026; IAEA, Nuclear Fuel Cycle Information System, section 'Electricity', consulted 16 November 2026.]
